title: How a City Gets Clean Water
production_path_basis: The source-to-tap system, barrier purposes, monitoring response, and safety boundaries must remain understandable without narration.
audience: General learners, families, and classroom audiences
assumed_knowledge: cities use pipes and treatment facilities
natural water may contain particles and microorganisms
central_message: Safe city-water delivery depends on a monitored sequence of distinct barriers and infrastructure, not one magical filter.
takeaway: Conventional treatment gathers and removes particles, adds microbial barriers, and continues through storage, distribution, monitoring, and maintenance.
platform: website showcase and bundled desktop example
scientific_depth: introductory conventional surface-water treatment, delivery infrastructure, turbidity-response workflow, and system boundaries
visual_direction: dark infrastructure tape with stable stage colors, semantic process nodes, numbered flow, and monitored response
pacing: tap-to-source overview, challenges, treatment train, stage purposes, monitoring, boundaries
constraints: do not imply every utility uses this exact train
do not provide operating or household-treatment instructions
do not imply disinfection removes every contaminant
success_criteria: eight stages remain ordered and traceable
each stage has a distinct visible purpose
safety and system limitations remain visible
